advances.name: Island Moat Defenses
advances.text: Ayutthaya sits at the confluence of three rivers, the Chao Phraya, Pa Sak, and Lopburi, on an artificial island created by digging canals to connect these waterways. This network of moats and channels makes the city virtually impregnable to conventional siege.

event.title: The Island Between Rivers
event.text:
Where the Chao Phraya, Pa Sak, and Lopburi rivers converge, our engineers have carved canals to complete what nature began. Ayutthaya now sits upon an island, surrounded on all sides by deep water, accessible only by boat or by bridges we control. No army can approach our walls without first crossing the rivers under our archers' fire. But this island is more than a fortress. The rivers that protect us also carry the trade of nations. Chinese junks, Indian dhows, and Malay praus crowd our wharves. We must decide: shall Ayutthaya be known as the impregnable citadel that none dare assault, or as the great crossroads where the wealth of Asia changes hands?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Let our moats be our ramparts.

modifiers.name: Impregnable Island
modifiers.text: Ayutthaya's water defenses make the capital a fortress without equal in Southeast Asia.

options.text: Let our rivers be our highways.

modifiers.name: River Crossroads
modifiers.text: The rivers of Ayutthaya carry the trade of nations, enriching all who dwell upon their banks.

advances.name: Khmer Inheritance
advances.text: The founders of Ayutthaya absorbed the administrative traditions of the declining Khmer Empire, adopting its court rituals, Sanskrit-derived titles, and hierarchical bureaucracy. The concept of the king as devaraja, a divine incarnation ruling from a cosmic center, gives Ayutthayan sovereignty a transcendent authority.

advances.name: Chao Phraya Flotilla
advances.text: Control of the Chao Phraya River is the lifeline of Ayutthaya. War boats patrol the waterways, intercept raiders, and escort merchant vessels through the kingdom's arterial river system.

advances.name: Dharmaraja Tradition
advances.text: King Ramathibodi I declared Theravada Buddhism the official religion of Ayutthaya in 1360 and brought monks from Ceylon to establish new orders. The Dharmaraja tradition blends Buddhist kingship with Brahmanical ritual, making the ruler both protector of the faith and a living embodiment of righteous law.

advances.name: Phrai Conscription
advances.text: Every freeman in Ayutthaya is registered as phrai, a subject obligated to provide corvee labor to the crown for half the year. This system, administered through local nai overlords, gives the king a vast pool of manpower for public works, military campaigns, and state construction projects.

advances.name: Cosmopolitan Entrepot
advances.text: Ayutthaya's location at the crossroads of maritime trade routes between China, India, and the spice islands draws merchants from across Asia. Foreign communities (Chinese, Indian, Persian, and later European) establish their own quarters outside the city walls, each governed by their own headman but contributing to the kingdom's treasury.

advances.name: Nihonmachi Quarter
advances.text: Japanese Christians and ronin fleeing the Tokugawa persecution establish a thriving quarter on the east bank of the Chao Phraya. At its peak in the 1620s, the Nihonmachi houses over 1,500 Japanese, including some six hundred warriors who serve the Siamese king as elite mercenaries. Their martial skill and discipline make them a formidable addition to the royal guard.

event.title: The Nihonmachi
event.text: A remarkable community has taken root on the east bank of the Chao Phraya, opposite the Portuguese quarter. Japanese Christians and masterless samurai, ronin, fleeing the Tokugawa Shogunate's persecution have established their own quarter, the Nihonmachi. Their headman governs by our leave, and their warriors have offered their swords in our service. These ronin are unlike any soldiers we have known: disciplined, fearless in close combat, and utterly loyal to whoever earns their respect. Already, nearly six hundred Japanese warriors drill in formation along the riverbank, their steel blades glinting in the tropical sun. The merchants among them deal in deer hides, sappanwood, and silk, enriching our treasury while their warriors strengthen our guard.

options.text: A worthy addition to our kingdom.

advances.name: Deerskin Export Trade
advances.text: Ayutthaya's forests teem with deer, and their hides are prized across East Asia. Japanese and Chinese merchants purchase thousands of skins annually for armor, clothing, and bookbinding. The deerskin trade becomes one of Ayutthaya's most profitable exports alongside sappanwood and rice.

advances.name: Palatine Law
advances.text: The codification of royal law establishes clear hierarchies of precedence, regulates the behavior of officials, and defines the duties owed by subjects to the crown. This legal framework, drawing on both Khmer tradition and Theravada Buddhist principles, will underpin Siamese governance for centuries.

advances.name: Royal War Barges
advances.text: The royal war barges of Ayutthaya are both weapons of war and symbols of majesty. Elaborately carved and gilded, these vessels carry musketeers and cannon on their prows while rowers propel them through the Chao Phraya with synchronized precision. A full procession of two hundred barges is a sight that awes foreign visitors and subjects alike.

units.name: Rua Rop
units.text: Shallow-draft war boats that patrol the Chao Phraya and its tributaries, carrying archers and musketeers to intercept raiders and pirates.

units.name: Phrai Lek
units.text: Conscript infantry drawn from the corvee labor system, these peasant soldiers serve their mandatory months in the royal armies.

units.name: Ronin Guard
units.text: Japanese masterless samurai who fled Tokugawa persecution and now serve the Ayutthayan king as elite foreign mercenaries, feared for their discipline and swordsmanship.

units.name: Rua Suwan Ratchakan
units.text: The gilded royal war barges of Ayutthaya, elaborately carved and equipped with bow-mounted cannon, used for both ceremonial processions and river combat.

buildings.name: Island Moat Fortress
buildings.text: A system of canals, moats, and water barriers exploiting Ayutthaya's island geography to create layered water defenses that make the city nearly impervious to siege.

buildings.name: Foreign Trading Quarter
buildings.text: A designated district outside the city walls where foreign merchants (Chinese, Indian, Persian, Japanese, and European) establish their own communities under the governance of appointed headmen.

buildings.name: Deerskin Yard
buildings.text: Hides brought down from the upland forests are dried, salted, sorted by grade and baled here for the ships that sail to Japan with the monsoon.

children.text: Wild Game is produced in the market

buildings.name: Royal Wat
buildings.text: A grand Buddhist temple complex serving as the spiritual heart of the kingdom, housing sacred relics, supporting monastic education, and legitimizing royal authority through religious patronage.

list.name: Krom Tha
list.text: Ayutthaya's maritime customs were uniquely organized into two co-equal port departments: the Krom Tha Khwa (Right Port), traditionally led by an officer of Chinese descent and managing East Asian traffic, and the Krom Tha Sai (Left Port), run by Persian Shia administrators (most famously the Bunnag family, descended from Sheikh Ahmad Qomi who arrived in 1602) and handling Indian, Persian, Arab, and European trade. The bifurcation gave the throne two parallel customs apparatuses and an institutionalized place for foreign-born officers in the highest ranks of court.

list.name: Tamruat Phon
list.text: The royal palace police: a guard corps within the Wang ministry distinct from the field army, recruited from trusted Mon and Khmer families and answerable only to the king and the Maha Uparat. The Tamruat Phon escorted the king during processions, conducted secret arrests of court rivals, and decided the outcome of every Ayutthayan succession crisis from Borommatrailokkanat through King Suriyamarin's deposition in 1767.

list.name: Yodfa Elephant Corps
list.text: After his 1593 single combat with the Burmese crown prince at Nong Sarai, King Naresuan reorganised the Ayutthayan elephant corps into a hereditary professional cadre. The Yodfa established war-elephant breeding stations in the upper Chao Phraya, mahout dynasties drawn from Lan Na and Lao client states, and a Mon refugee pikeman escort granted Ayutthayan land in exchange for service. The corps fielded Ayutthaya's most reliable infantry through the 17th century, fending off the Toungoo invasions and projecting suzerainty into Cambodia and the northern Malay sultanates.

list.name: Krom Mahatlek
list.text: The royal pages court enrolled the sons of Ayutthayan nobles, vassal rulers, and high-ranking foreign officers as boys serving in the inner palace. Pages slept on the floor outside the king's chambers, ran his messages, and learned governance by observing council. On reaching majority they entered the four-pillar ministries as junior officers, ensuring that the next generation of governors had been personally vetted by the throne. The system also functioned as a hostage apparatus: a rebellious vassal's son was always a sword's-stroke from the king's guard.

list.name: Kromakan Asa
list.text: More than any other Southeast Asian state, Ayutthaya integrated foreign-born officers into its upper administration. The Kromakan Asa enrolled Persians under Sheikh Ahmad Qomi (1602), the Japanese Yamada Nagamasa as governor of Nakhon Si Thammarat in the 1620s, the Greek Constantine Phaulkon as Phra Khlang under King Narai (1685-88), Portuguese gunners at the Asa Cherokat artillery park, and French engineers under Desfarges in 1687. Each foreigner was granted Sakdina rank and a Krom of his own client community, opening unique channels for firearms, fortification science, and Persian Gulf diplomacy.
